title: People may feel better after leaving a platform while social dependence makes leaving hard
source_unit: World Happiness Report 2026 Chapter 6 synthesis of published Facebook deactivation and U.S. college-student collective-exit studies; component studies are retained as distinct populations and designs
geography: United States; Facebook-user experiment and U.S. college-student Instagram/TikTok coordination study

observations.period: Facebook deactivation experiment; four-week intervention reported in World Happiness Report 2026

denominator.unit: Facebook users recruited for the Allcott et al. experiment

deactivation_effect.value: those assigned to deactivate for four weeks were happier, more satisfied with life, less anxious, and less depressed on measured outcomes

later_use.value: the deactivation group later reported lower Facebook use and was more likely to delete the app

political_knowledge.value: the control group had significantly more political knowledge than the deactivation group in the reported measures

durable_exit.unit: long-run account closure, replacement, civic participation, or stable non-use

observations.method: World Happiness Report synthesis of Allcott et al.'s randomized four-week Facebook deactivation experiment; treatment and control groups are kept separate from the report's other studies.
observations.uncertainty: The experiment concerns recruited Facebook users and a short intervention. The report does not make it a representative estimate of all U.S. adults, and improved subjective wellbeing does not capture every valued connection, information benefit, or material consequence.
observations.subgroup: Facebook users in the experiment; the public chapter does not provide a general-population estimate or a same-person link to the separate Instagram/TikTok coordination study.
observations.counterinterpretation: A person can be less anxious while offline and still value political information, social connection, or practical coordination enough to return. App deletion is not proof of permanent account exit.

observations.period: U.S. college-student collective-exit study summarized in World Happiness Report 2026

denominator.unit: substantial sample of U.S. college students; exact denominator not stated in the public chapter passage used here

individual_exit_value.value: many participants would demand payment to give up Instagram or TikTok for a month when others' use remained unchanged

collective_exit_value.value: many participants would instead pay to eliminate the platform from their community when everyone else was asked to leave too

coordination_mechanism.value: the report interprets the difference as social dependence or a negative non-user externality
coordination_mechanism.unit: reported interpretation of a conditional experiment

actual_collective_exit.unit: real-world coordinated deletion, substitution, or community-wide non-use

observations.method: World Happiness Report synthesis of a U.S. college-student conditional valuation study; this is not pooled with the Facebook deactivation experiment.
observations.uncertainty: Willingness to pay or accept is a stated valuation, not observed deletion or durable behavior. The college setting, hypothetical coordination condition, and platform-specific context limit generalization.
observations.subgroup: U.S. college students in the underlying study; not all U.S. users and not the same participants as the Facebook experiment.
observations.counterinterpretation: A collective-exit preference can reflect dislike of social pressure without proving that the platform causes harm, that all users want to leave, or that coordination would be feasible.

related_sources.claim: The NBER platform time-cost experiments are a separate platform-demand and time-allocation source; they are not merged with the deactivation or collective-exit studies.

boundary: This record adds a platform-exit and collective-coordination mechanism. It does not establish a population-wide causal effect of social media, a durable exit rate, a complete welfare balance, a political-action effect, or a recommendation about platform policy. The two component studies use different samples, platforms, outcomes, and designs.
